channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Food & Agriculture
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Ransomware against food and agriculture is up 62%, and the groups doing it schedule around harvest — which has just started
item.category: Top Story
item.description: An Industrial Cyber analysis published on 8 September, built on Food and Ag-ISAC sector data, puts ransomware against food and agriculture at 227 incidents through July 2026, a 62% rise year on year and enough to make this the eighth most-targeted industry. Qilin, Akira, CL0P, Play and Lynx are named as the leading groups against the sector, and the ISAC separately records Iranian activity against internet-exposed programmable logic controllers in food-processing and grain-handling systems specifically. The finding that should change planning is the timing one. Analysts assess that actors deliberately schedule campaigns around planting and harvest, and the September–November harvest window — when elevators, processing plants and cold-chain operators run at maximum throughput with the least tolerance for downtime — opened during this reporting period. The consequence argument is the other half, and it is the part that separates this sector from the rest of manufacturing. Loss of cold-chain and refrigeration telemetry forces product disposal regardless of whether the product was ever actually out of temperature, because compliance cannot be demonstrated without a continuous record. Compromise of production, quality or traceability data is treated by regulators as a food-safety event that triggers holds or recalls, not as an IT outage. This is analysis and sector data, not a report of a specific compromise. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis drawing on Food and Ag-ISAC sector data — ransomware counts and named actors originate in the ISAC’s 3 September report - Feature published 8 Sep 2026; underlying ISAC report 3 Sep 2026; ransomware figures cover January–July 2026

item.title: [Critical] A China-linked actor emptied the code repositories of an industrial automation firm — SCADA and HMI tooling, not customer data
item.category: Incident — State-linked campaign, confirmed compromise, SCADA and HMI source code stolen
item.description: Acronis’s Threat Research Unit published research on 13 September on an actor it calls Red Heron, which has been exploiting a critical remote-code-execution flaw in the self-hosted Gitea code platform, CVE-2026-60004, since 29 July. The campaign scanned 1,386 self-hosted Gitea instances across seven countries and produced confirmed compromises at no fewer than 11 organisations — Industrial Cyber reports 11 targets in five countries, while The Hacker News reports 13 in six. The two that matter to industrial readers are a Taiwanese industrial automation company, whose stolen repositories covered SCADA and HMI tooling, IoT platform integrations and network-sniffer products, and a Canadian renewable-energy firm, from which infrastructure maps, configuration secrets, SSH host keys and internal tokens were taken. The actor installed a custom implant the researchers call JITTERLY alongside a Linux rootkit supporting more than thirty post-exploitation commands. Attribution to a Chinese-speaking group is moderate confidence, based on language artefacts and tradecraft, and Acronis does not tie it to a known APT group; the apparent aim is espionage and source-code theft, not ransomware. No food or agriculture victim is named. The reason it belongs on this page is the target class: a food plant’s process knowledge does not only live in the plant. It lives in the machine builder’s and integrator’s repositories — PLC and HMI projects, recipe and batch logic, refrigeration control code, and the credentials commissioning engineers left in them. - Acronis Threat Research Unit report — reported by The Hacker News and Industrial Cyber, KEV dates per SecurityWeek; attribution assessed at moderate confidence by the researchers - Research published 13 Sep 2026; media reporting 14–15 Sep 2026; exploitation observed from 29 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] The dump after a refused ransom included infrastructure vulnerability analyses and plaintext credentials
item.category: Incident — Refusal to pay, then publication of infrastructure documentation
item.description: Rhysida published the data it took from Berlin’s state administration on 4 September after the city declined a demand reported at 30 bitcoin. The claimed set runs to about 5.79 TB across roughly 1.44 million files and, beyond personnel and payroll records, is reported to include critical-infrastructure vulnerability analyses — among them assessments of the city’s water supply — along with plaintext credentials for administrator accounts and connected systems. Berlin detected data leaving on 7 August, outflow continued to around 12 August, and the affected departments were not physically disconnected until 14 August. Food and beverage operators sit in an unusually documented supply chain: audit files, HACCP and food-defence plans, line layouts, refrigeration and utility drawings, and OEM remote-access credentials are routinely shared with co-packers, certification bodies, equipment vendors and retail customers. A breach at any one of them publishes your plant without anyone touching it. - Berlin state administration statements — reported by Help Net Security and Security Affairs - Breach and refusal to pay reported 1 Sep 2026; data published by the actor 4 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] A phone call, not an exploit — a distributor’s SSO accounts were talked open, then used against Salesforce and Snowflake
item.category: Incident — Identity-based intrusion at a major distributor
item.description: McKesson disclosed on 31 August that it had discovered a cybersecurity incident on 25 August. ShinyHunters claims responsibility and says it took roughly a terabyte over four days — about 284 million records — with a demand near $55 million; the company states it has not determined the incident to be material. What matters outside healthcare is the route in: voice phishing against employees, leading to compromised Okta single sign-on accounts, and from there into the company’s Salesforce and Snowflake tenants. No software flaw was involved. Food and agriculture runs on the same shape of estate — a distribution business joined to growers, co-packers and retailers by SaaS, with order, forecast and traceability data pooled in cloud analytics platforms behind one identity provider and one help desk. - McKesson SEC filing and company statement, plus threat-actor claims reported by BleepingComputer — corroborated by Help Net Security, SC Media and HIPAA Journal - Incident discovered 25 Aug 2026; disclosed and reported 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Ransomware against manufacturers is up 40% this year, and the growth has moved to Europe
item.category: Research — Vendor report, leak-site counts, no named food victim
item.description: Black Kite’s 2026 Manufacturing and Distribution Ransomware Report, covered on 17 September, counts 1,183 new ransomware incidents against manufacturers in the first seven months of 2026 — a 40% rise on the same period in 2025, and part of 5,237 disclosed victims across manufacturing and distribution since January 2023. The geography has shifted: the United States accounts for 412 attacks, still the largest single share at 35% but down from 52%, while Europe rose 85% to 369 (Germany 77, Italy 57, the UK 43, France 40) and the rest of the world nearly doubled to 402. Qilin leads the actor table, followed by The Gentlemen — a group with 142 claimed manufacturing victims by mid-2026, about 12% of the year’s total — then Akira, DragonForce and INC Ransom. About half of this year’s attacks came from groups that did not exist two years ago. Distribution logged 95 incidents in the first half of 2026 against 196 for the whole of 2025. Two caveats matter before anyone quotes this at a board. These are leak-site and disclosure counts, which measure claimed victims rather than confirmed OT-disruptive incidents. And the report covers manufacturing and distribution as a whole: food and beverage production sits inside that population, but the coverage gives no food-specific figures, so treat the trend as directional for this sector rather than as a sector count. - Black Kite 2026 Manufacturing and Distribution Ransomware Report — figures as reported by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber; the report itself was not read directly - Reported 17 Sep 2026; figures cover January–July 2026 against the same period in 2025

item.title: [Medium] August set a global ransomware record at 997 attacks, with utilities among the categories driving the rise
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — an average of 32 a day, a 23 percent increase on July’s 809, and above the previous monthly record of 988. The reporting singles out utility, healthcare and business-services attacks as the categories behind the surge. Treat the absolute number with the usual caution — counts of this kind depend on leak-site claims and disclosure practice as much as on actual incident volume, and claimed victims are not confirmed victims. The direction of travel, however, is consistent with what operators are seeing. Food and beverage processors sit inside the manufacturing and business-services categories behind this record. The sector's own history — production stoppages that begin as IT events — is exactly the pattern the numbers describe. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Data for August 2026; reporting published 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Cyber-informed engineering argues the useful question is not how to keep attackers out, but which consequences you can design away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analysis, engineering practice
item.description: An analysis published 15 September sets out the case for cyber-informed engineering in critical infrastructure: that industrial systems operate under a constraint IT does not share, because a compromised network does not automatically have to become a catastrophic physical event. The argument is to move the security question upstream into design — identifying the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineering them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system remaining trustworthy. For food and beverage the consequence is a safety one, not just a production one: a compromised control system that produces an out-of-spec batch or a cold-chain excursion becomes a public-health problem. The argument is that engineered limits — mechanical stops, independent temperature cut-outs, physical verification steps — do more than any detection tool. This is practitioner analysis rather than incident reporting; it names no victim and describes no attack, but it is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - Industrial Cyber feature analysis on cyber-informed engineering - Published 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Google’s threat group saw a credential-harvesting campaign run end to end by autonomous agents in under six hours
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Autonomous agent tooling in a live campaign
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated actor ran a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign using an autonomous multi-agent framework, completing it in less than six hours. GTIG also describes actors going after proprietary AI models across healthcare, government and media, stealing API credentials and co-opting victim cloud environments to run their own AI workloads at the victim’s expense. GTIG’s John Hultquist frames the takeaway bluntly: assume every threat actor is using AI in some capacity. For food and agriculture the significance is speed rather than novelty. Credential theft against corporate accounts is already the documented route into distribution, ordering and plant-adjacent systems in this sector, and a campaign that completes inside a shift compresses the window in which a lean plant IT team could plausibly notice and intervene. - Google Threat Intelligence Group reporting — as covered by The Hacker News - Published 8 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Food and Ag-ISAC: confirmed attacks on exposed plant-floor PLCs, and a “shadow OT” estate nobody has counted
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Sector threat report, confirmed PLC exposure
item.description: The Food and Ag-ISAC published its State of the Threat report on 3 September, and the operational findings matter more than the totals. Federal agencies have confirmed attacks on internet-exposed programmable logic controllers running processing lines and grain-handling equipment; hacktivist crews such as Dark Engine have demonstrated they can reach HMIs controlling automated machinery, irrigation and temperature-controlled storage; and the ISAC warns that “shadow OT” — networked silo sensors, automated feeders and cold-chain thermometers added for efficiency and never inventoried — is growing faster than most teams can track it. On volume, ransomware against food and agriculture reached 227 incidents through July, up 62% year on year, with Qilin (47), The Gentlemen (31) and Akira (14) the most active groups, making this the eighth most-targeted sector. - Food and Ag-ISAC “State of the Threat: Food and Agriculture Sector Cyber Trends” report, produced with the IT-ISAC — reported by Industrial Cyber - Report published and reported 3 Sep 2026; ransomware figures cover January–July 2026

item.title: [Medium] The way in is still somebody you already trust — contractor accounts and standing remote access top the entry-path list
item.category: Threat intel — vendor telemetry on industrial attack volume and entry paths; contractor access and trusted remote access lead
item.description: Industrial Cyber reported on 4 September that the security firm F6 ranks manufacturing as the most-attacked sector in its 2026 telemetry and finds roughly 80% of the industrial organisations in its customer base short of qualified security staff. The entry paths it singles out are ones a food or beverage processor should recognise immediately: contractor compromise and trusted remote access — legitimate credentials belonging to somebody the plant already lets in, rather than an exploit against the line. Its recommendations are operational: unified telemetry across IT and OT, fast reconstruction of an intrusion chain, alert correlation, and dedicated monitoring of contractor sessions. This is one vendor’s data from one region and the ranking is directional at best, but the contractor-access finding matches what Dragos and the Food and Ag-ISAC have both reported about this sector’s ransomware cases. - F6 research reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published telemetry from one firm’s customer base; treat the ranking as directional rather than a global count - Reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Eighteen frontier models were run at a real enterprise network — one completed the whole kill chain unaided
item.category: Research — measured autonomous attack capability in frontier AI models; no incident
item.description: Booz Allen published its Cyber Weapon Index and an accompanying report on 4 September, grading eighteen frontier AI models on how much of an intrusion they can carry out without a human driving. The models were run against a representative enterprise network rather than a benchmark; the top performer completed the full sequence — reconnaissance, initial access, lateral movement and objective — unaided, while most managed individual stages. The authors’ conclusion is about time rather than novelty: nothing in the tested behaviour was a new technique, but the interval between a foothold and a consequence compresses when the attacker never pauses to think. Booz Allen also reports that defensive playbooks written specifically against autonomous attackers cut their success rate by more than 95% in the same tests. For a processor running lines round the clock with a lean security team, the exposure is the night shift: an attacker that does not tire reaches line control long before anyone reads the alert queue in the morning. - Booz Allen Cyber Weapon Index and the report “The Offensive Frontier: AI as the Attacker”, reported by Industrial Cyber — vendor-published research; the figures are the authors’ own test results and have not been independently reproduced - Published and reported 4 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Fire Ant compromises the routers and login servers that sit between plants, cold stores and head office
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Nation-state intrusion at the network layer
item.description: Sygnia published research on 30 August showing the China-nexus group it tracks as Fire Ant has moved out of VMware hypervisors and into the network layer: Cisco IOS XR routers, TACACS authentication servers and Linux management hosts inside a large interconnected estate. Router implants suppressed selected syslog messages and served interactive shells that logged nothing; on TACACS the actor injected a library into the running daemon and copied administrator credentials as logins were approved. Sygnia observed scanning and connection attempts toward linked critical-infrastructure networks without confirming compromise there. Food and beverage sites rarely own that layer. The routers joining a processing plant, a distribution centre and head office are usually run by corporate IT or a provider — and the logs that would show tampering come from those same devices, which is precisely what this actor set out to make unreliable. - Sygnia research publication and press release — corroborated by BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, Cybersecurity Dive and SC Media - Sygnia published 30 Aug 2026; wider reporting 31 Aug 2026

item.title: [Info] Six steps to being able to disconnect the plant — and a three-month planning horizon
item.category: Research — Isolation readiness, practitioner guidance
item.description: Nozomi Networks published a practitioner summary on 2 September of the Five Eyes “CI Fortify” guidance released in late July, reducing it to six steps: identify vital systems and their dependencies; establish trust levels and connection maps; pre-build the separation points; create and test graduated isolation plans; retain visibility while isolated; and run post-isolation checks before reconnecting. Food and beverage plants tend to discover their dependency map the hard way, because the enterprise side holds recipe management, allergen and label data, lot genealogy and cold-chain monitoring — systems you cannot legally or safely run without, even if the line itself would keep turning. Nozomi’s planning horizon of up to three months of isolated operation is worth using as a tabletop prompt: how long can you make, label and release product with the enterprise layer unavailable? - Nozomi Networks Labs analysis of the CISA / ASD ACSC / NCSC-UK / CCCS “CI Fortify” guidance - Analysis published 2 Sep 2026; underlying guidance published 28 Jul 2026

item.title: [High] Researchers moved a working PLC exploit to a sibling controller with an AI model — and permanently bricked one
item.category: Research — AI-assisted exploit porting against PLCs
item.description: Forescout’s Vedere Labs set a large language model the task of taking a working remote-code-execution exploit for one WAGO controller — the 750-852, via CVE-2021-31886, a pre-authentication buffer overflow in its Nucleus FTP server — and re-targeting it at a related model, the 750-831. It worked, but not cheaply or unattended: the final stage alone ran more than eight hours and over $500 in API costs, with a researcher steering throughout. A later session aimed at building a command-and-control implant wrote a payload into flash-mapped memory and permanently bricked the test controller. For a processor the relevant risk is the mixed estate — batching, CIP skids, packaging and refrigeration rarely share one controller model, and the assumption that a published exploit stops at the model boundary is weaker than it was. - Forescout Vedere Labs research reported by SecurityWeek - Reported 1 Sep 2026; underlying flaw CVE-2021-31886 disclosed 2021

item.title: [Critical] NCSC issues an alert: increased targeting of OT across multiple sectors globally, and it has already caused real-world disruption
item.category: Threat Intelligence — National agency alert on OT targeting
item.description: The NCSC published a formal alert on 27 August stating it has seen increased targeting of operational technology across multiple sectors globally, including in the UK, by a range of threat actors, and that the activity has caused some limited real-world disruption. No victims, actors or techniques are named. Food and agriculture is not called out, but the exposure pattern is the sector’s to a fault. The NCSC’s instruction — do not assume your OT is unreachable from the internet without verifying it, because exposure arises through misconfiguration, legacy connections and unmanaged assets — describes the packaging line an OEM supports over its own 4G router, the refrigeration and CIP controllers commissioned by a contractor, the grain elevator and cold-store telemetry on a cellular link, and the plant acquired with a business and never brought under a standard build. Advisory AA26-231A already names food and agriculture among the sectors where S7 controllers are being read. - UK National Cyber Security Centre alert, “Disruptive cyber activity highlights risk from internet-exposed systems and edge devices” - Published 27 Aug 2026; the NCSC says it has been engaging affected sectors directly ahead of publication

item.title: [High] A ransomware affiliate ran an AI coding agent inside victim networks — and the exposed server shows exactly how
item.category: Threat Intel — Ransomware tradecraft, AI-assisted intrusion
item.description: CloudSEK published analysis on 27 August of a misconfigured server belonging to a Russian-speaking Aurora ransomware affiliate, exposing tooling, command history, credential material and the operator’s Cursor chat transcripts. The campaign ran from April to July 2026 across nine countries; the operator reached domain-level or interactive access at 17 organisations, and four appeared on Aurora’s leak site. Food, agriculture, manufacturing and professional-services organisations were among those affected, which puts this page’s audience squarely in the targeting set. The notable detail is not that AI was used but where: the transcripts show the assistant helping plan Active Directory escalation and intrusion steps, compressing the time between initial access and domain control. For a processor the useful question is whether the domain account your IT team uses every day can also authenticate to the MES, the batch server or a line HMI, because this operator reached victims through domain privilege rather than any control-system exploit. - CloudSEK research published 27 Aug 2026 — corroborated by GBHackers and Cybersecurity News - Research published 27 Aug 2026; the intrusion activity it documents ran April to July 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 bypass in Cisco ISE — the box that decides which devices are allowed onto the plant network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited as a zero-day, KEV-listed, three-day federal deadline
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, an authentication bypass rated CVSS 10.0 in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker reach the web-based management interface, and Cisco states its PSIRT “is aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability”. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — the interim control is infrastructure access lists restricting management traffic. CISA added the CVE to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 September with a federal remediation deadline of 19 September, a three-day window. No attacker attribution has been published, and no critical-infrastructure or industrial targeting is claimed. The reason it sits on a food and beverage page is what ISE usually does in these estates: it is the network access control and 802.1X policy engine that decides which laptops, contractor devices and plant machines are admitted to which VLAN, and it frequently underwrites the remote-access authorisation at the industrial DMZ. An attacker with administrative control of that policy engine does not need a plant exploit to reach the line. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA KEV catalog — corroborated by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory published 16 Sep 2026; KEV listing 16 Sep 2026, federal deadline 19 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Six CISA ICS advisories on 17 September, and the PLC engineering software is the one to read first
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA released six industrial control system advisories on 17 September, ICSA-26-260-01 through -06: Bransys ELD, Mitsubishi Electric GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings, Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform, Schneider Electric Modicon M340 controllers and communication modules, Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 (750 and 755) and ABB Ability Edgenius. The only score we can verify in the batch is Mitsubishi’s: CVE-2026-15688, an authentication algorithm flaw in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings rated CVSS v3.1 8.8 and v4.0 8.7, affecting all versions. The Bransys ELD advisory covers three hardcoded or cleartext credential issues in an electronic logging device for commercial trucking, fixed in Android 11.00.00 and iOS 1.1.54. CISA reports no exploitation for anything in the batch. Separately, CISA updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN) on 17 September to add eight affected products. Scores and CISA sector lists for the Hitachi Energy, Schneider and ABB advisories had not reached the public CSAF mirror at the time of writing, so they are deliberately not quoted here. For food and beverage readers the relevant pair is editorial rather than official: Modicon M340 is a common process and discrete controller on plant lines, and GX Works3 is the engineering software used to write and load Mitsubishi PLC logic — an authentication weakness there is a control-program integrity question, not only a workstation one. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -06 — CVE detail for -01 and -02 from the CISA CSAF record; scores for -03 to -06 not yet published in the public mirror and therefore not quoted - Advisories released 17 Sep 2026; ICSA-26-211-07 updated the same day

item.title: [Critical] One firmware, three vendors: CVSS 9.8 flaws in the IO-Link masters that sit on packaging and process lines
item.category: Advisory — Shared IO-Link master firmware across three vendors, fixes available, no reported exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published three coordinated advisories on 16 September for IO-Link master devices built on a common firmware older than 1.7.4: Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8 (VDE-2026-027), Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2 and ICE3 modules (VDE-2026-014) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 devices (VDE-2026-028), all three carrying the same set of about 20 CVEs (CVE-2026-27546 to CVE-2026-27565). The two worst are rated CVSS 9.8: CVE-2026-27546, an unauthenticated bypass that grants administrator access, and CVE-2026-27565, which lets an unauthenticated attacker upload a malicious IODD device-description file that runs a shell script as root. Many further command-injection flaws score 8.8, and the set also exposes password hashes and SSH private keys. Phoenix Contact’s advisory credits Nozomi Networks. No exploitation is reported, and fixed firmware 1.7.8 is available. IO-Link masters are the gateways between the plant network and the sensors and actuators on automated equipment, which in a food or beverage plant often means filling, packaging, palletising and conveying machinery delivered by a machine builder. That is why the practical question is less “do we own these?” than “did our OEMs build them in?”. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-027 (Phoenix Contact), VDE-2026-014 (Pepperl+Fuchs) and VDE-2026-028 (Carlo Gavazzi) - Advisories published 16 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] mySCADA myPRO Manager flaw rated CVSS 9.8 opens management functions and the SMS alarm modem
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS advisory naming Food and Agriculture, fix available, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03, released on 15 September, covers mySCADA myPRO Manager version 2.1 and earlier. CVE-2026-73807 is a missing-authorization flaw rated CVSS v3 9.8, and CVE-2026-82567 is a missing-authentication flaw in a critical function rated 6.3. According to CISA, they could let an attacker reach privileged management functions or send arbitrary SMS messages through a GSM modem connected to the system. CISA lists Food and Agriculture among the affected sectors, alongside critical manufacturing, energy, transportation and water. The fix is version 2.2, and CISA reports no known public exploitation. The SMS detail is the sector-relevant one: smaller processors, cold stores and agricultural sites often rely on text alerts for out-of-hours alarms, so a channel an outsider can write to is a channel staff may stop trusting. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-258-03 (CSAF record in CISA’s GitHub repository) - Advisory released 15 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] September’s ICS patch wave lands in the process-control layer that also enforces food safety
item.category: Advisory — September ICS patch wave, vendor fixes available, no reported exploitation
item.description: Schneider Electric and Siemens both shipped critical fixes on 8 September. The most consequential for food and beverage plants is a critical authentication vulnerability in Modicon M580 and M580 Safety controllers, CVE-2026-3869 at CVSS 9.2 — the safety variant is the part worth pausing on. Siemens published seven advisories the same day, spanning Reyrolle protection relays, Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager. Both arrive on top of the 3 September Inductive Automation Ignition flaw, CVE-2026-77393 at CVSS 8.8, which sits in the HMI and SCADA layer of a great many processing sites. None is reported exploited. What makes this a sector story rather than a patch list is the point Industrial Cyber made on 8 September: in food manufacturing, process control is food-safety control. Cook and pasteurisation setpoints, chemical dosing, cold-chain holds and batch integrity all live there. - Schneider Electric and Siemens ProductCERT security notifications, CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-246-06 for Ignition — round-up reporting by SecurityWeek, sector framing from Industrial Cyber - Vendor advisories published 8 Sep 2026; Ignition advisory published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] GitLab CVSS 10 path traversal is being exploited, and food and beverage teams host more of it than they think
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: GitLab patched CVE-2026-85706 on 10 September, a path-traversal flaw in the repository commits API that it rated CVSS 10.0 and that allows an unauthenticated attacker to read arbitrary files from a GitLab server. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Friday 11 September with a remediation deadline for federal agencies of Monday 14 September. watchTowr reported it was already seeing in-the-wild probes for vulnerable servers, and Hong Kong’s CERT issued its own advisory on 14 September stating the flaw is being exploited in the wild. A second flaw fixed in the same release, CVE-2026-87719, can expose sensitive information from Enterprise Edition servers. Food and beverage processors version recipe management, batch control integrations, MES and warehouse-management interfaces, and cold-chain telemetry code in self-hosted GitLab. Unauthenticated reads against that repository expose both the process knowledge and the service credentials that reach packaging lines and refrigeration control. - GitLab patch release advisory and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — reporting via Cybersecurity Dive - GitLab patch published 10 Sep 2026; KEV listing 11 Sep 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi’s second SCALANCE LPE9403 study: 12 flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device
item.category: Advisory — Vendor-patched vulnerability research, chainable to root, no reported exploitation
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published the second part of its Siemens SCALANCE LPE9403 research on 18 September, bringing the total to 12 vulnerabilities — nine in the device firmware and three in the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client, scored between CVSS 5.3 and 8.5. Firmware below V4.0 HF0 and Edge Client releases through V2.1 are affected, and Siemens has published an advisory and patches; V4.0 HF0 and later carry the fixes. The finding that matters is not any single score: Nozomi demonstrated that several of the flaws can be chained to obtain root-level control of the device, which would allow manipulation of telemetry, suppression of alarms, access to operational data, disruption of OT services and lateral movement onto connected networks. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild. Two dates are worth keeping straight, because the coverage has muddled them. The first part of this research, published 10 September, described four PROFINET DCP denial-of-service flaws rated CVSS 5.3 (CVE-2025-40575 to CVE-2025-40578) in a daemon that runs as root without authentication on every device interface. The underlying CVEs were originally disclosed in May 2025 under CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18; what happened on 15 September was an update to that advisory adding the SINEMA Remote Connect Edge Client and vendor fixes, not a new critical vulnerability. Processing and packaging lines that use the LPE9403 to aggregate PROFINET data for MES or cloud analytics should read the chained-root result as the reason to close the firmware gap rather than defer it. - Nozomi Networks Labs research, parts one and two, and Siemens ProductCERT SSA-327438 / CISA ICSA-25-135-18 — reporting via Industrial Cyber; the full 12-CVE identifier list has not been re-verified against Siemens’ advisory here, so it is not reproduced - Part one published 10 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-25-135-18 updated 15 Sep 2026; part two published 18 Sep 2026; underlying CVEs first disclosed May 2025

item.title: [Critical] A ransomware operator is picking encryption targets from inside Cisco firewall management — that is how a plant stops
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is being exploited in the wild. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the underlying operating system. Cisco patched it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos reports three clusters. UAT-12197, unattributed, exploited CVE-2026-20079 and deployed a web shell and malicious JAR to harvest credentials. UAT-11823, an APT cluster that exploited both CVE-2026-20079 and the earlier CVE-2026-20316, is Sandworm-linked through tooling overlap and deployed a Cyclops Blink variant. UAT-11988, a ransomware operator, came in only through CVE-2026-20316 using static credentials, performed reconnaissance and compiled endpoint lists for encryption, and ultimately deployed Qilin. Food and beverage operators should read the Qilin detail literally. The sector’s production stoppages this year have followed that shape — enterprise intrusion, target enumeration, then encryption reaching the systems batching, packaging and refrigeration depend on. FMC is where the boundary meant to prevent that is configured. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; KEV federal remediation deadline falls 12 Sep 2026 — re-checked 11 Sep 2026, no further change of state

item.title: [Critical] The MikroTik router chain moved from disclosed to exploited — unauthenticated admin over SSH
item.category: Critical Advisory — Now confirmed exploited in the wild
item.description: CERT Polska issued an alert on 9 September confirming that the MikroTik RouterOS flaws known as the “MikroTrick” chain, previously disclosed but not confirmed exploited, are now being used in real-world attacks observed since at least 2 September. The chain pairs an SSH authentication bypass, CVE-2026-67276 at CVSS 9.2, with an SSH privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-86060 also at CVSS 9.2, to take full unauthenticated administrative control of an internet-exposed RouterOS device; a third bug, CVE-2026-67277, allows memory disclosure or denial of service through the bandwidth-test service. CERT Polska named no victims and no sectors, noting only that MikroTik devices are widely deployed by ISPs, data centres, enterprises and critical-infrastructure networks. This is a change of exploitation status, not a new vulnerability. It is on this page for the same reason the Cisco item is: the box sitting between a remote site and everything else is usually the cheapest thing in the estate and the least likely to be on anyone’s asset register. - CERT Polska alert — reported by Industrial Cyber - Alert published 9 Sep 2026; exploitation observed from at least 2 Sep 2026; CISA KEV listing 12 Sep 2026, federal deadline 13 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Dutch NCSC expects imminent attacks on two CVSS 9.8 Check Point VPN flaws — patches landed 9 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — VPN gateway, exploitation assessed imminent
item.description: The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre warned, in reporting published 12 September, that it expects near-term exploitation attempts against two critical Check Point VPN vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-85102 and CVE-2026-85103, both rated CVSS 9.8. They can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on Security Gateways, and a certificate-decoding defect can also affect Security Management Servers. Check Point released fixes on 9 September. Nothing is confirmed exploited and no public exploit code had been reported when the warning was issued — this is a forecast from a national CSIRT and is recorded as one. For a food or beverage business the exposure is the shape of the estate rather than the product: processing plants, distribution centres, leased cold stores and co-packers are usually stitched together by site-to-site tunnels on a small number of gateways, and the same gateways carry the OEM paths to filling, packaging and refrigeration controls. One gateway typically stands between a corporate network and every plant floor in the group. - Dutch National Cyber Security Centre warning — reported by BleepingComputer. Assessed as imminent; no confirmed exploitation and no food-sector victims named - Check Point fixes released 9 Sep 2026; NCSC warning reported 12 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds five exploited flaws to KEV — including the tool your line OEM dials in with at 3 am
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-support tooling
item.description: CISA added five vulnerabilities affecting JFrog Artifactory, ConnectWise ScreenConnect and MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 12 September after evidence of active exploitation, with federal remediation deadlines of 13 September for RouterOS, 14 September for ScreenConnect and 25 September for Artifactory. Reporting indicates the Artifactory flaws were chained to obtain administrator control, establish persistence and install Rust-based backdoors; ScreenConnect exploitation reportedly enabled unauthorised file transfer and execution through active sessions using a malicious VBScript payload. The RouterOS entry is the CERT Polska chain carried separately here. ScreenConnect is the one that matters most on a food page. Filling, labelling, palletising and refrigeration vendors support their equipment remotely, often out of hours during a run, and the agent that makes that possible is usually installed at commissioning on the same PC that programs the line. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition — reported by The Hacker News - KEV addition 12 Sep 2026; reporting 13 Sep 2026; federal deadlines 13, 14 and 25 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in the RMM platform that manages plant IT — plus two Windows zero-days and a Magento bug
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV
item.description: CISA added four vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 8 September, all with vendor patches already available. The one to act on first is CVE-2026-86218 in N-able N-central, scored CVSS 10.0: a static code injection issue giving pre-authentication remote code execution. N-able has confirmed exploitation in the wild, Huntress observed attacks against N-central’s API and appliance logs from 4 September, and N-able shipped 2026.3 Hotfix 4 on 5 September — its fourth hotfix in five weeks. The federal remediation deadline was 11 September and has now passed. Also added: CVE-2026-81963 and CVE-2026-85880, both Windows privilege-escalation zero-days reaching SYSTEM, and CVE-2026-75650, a CVSS 10.0 template-engine injection in Adobe Commerce and Magento that Adobe confirms is being used against merchants. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 8 Sep 2026, with N-able, Microsoft and Adobe advisories — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer and CyberScoop - Added to KEV 8 Sep 2026; N-able hotfix released 5 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] The rest of the September patch wave: Siemens Reyrolle, Industrial Edge Management and hardcoded keys in Aveva
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patches available, no reported exploitation
item.description: Beyond the Modicon and Ignition items, the 8 September wave carried several findings worth logging even where the equipment is not on a food line. Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 covers fourteen CVEs in Reyrolle 7SR5 protection and control relays, all versions before V2.70; the lead flaw, CVE-2026-62645 at CVSS v3.1 9.8, lets an attacker derive current and past session identifiers from data the web interface leaks and bypass authentication. Weak session entropy and a role-based access control bypass granting administrator rights sit alongside it. Siemens issued nine advisories in total, also naming Open Interface Services, Industrial Edge Management and SIMOVE Fleetmanager, and began shipping fixes for Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431. Aveva disclosed four flaws in the PIMBoards component of Pipeline Integrity Monitor, including a hardcoded encryption key and MD5 password hashing; CISA formalised those on 10 September as advisory ICSA-26-253-01 — CVE-2026-81821 and CVE-2026-81822 both at CVSS v3 8.4, CVE-2026-81823 at 5.3 and CVE-2026-81824 at 4.7, affecting versions up to and including 2025_SP1_P1 and fixed in the 2025 SP1 P2 security update. It was the only new ICS advisory CISA published in the 9–11 September window. None is reported exploited. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-142885 and the wider September ProductCERT set, with Aveva security bulletin AVEVA-2026-006 and CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 — round-up reporting by SecurityWeek and ISSSource - Advisories published 8 Sep 2026 (SSA-142885 v1.0); CISA advisory ICSA-26-253-01 for Aveva Pipeline Integrity Monitor published 10 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 3 September batch hits the integrator’s toolkit — IXON VPN client, Rockwell ControlFLASH, Ignition
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access client, firmware tool and SCADA platform
item.description: CISA published a further set of ICS advisories on 3 September, and all three of the notable ones live in the system integrator’s toolkit rather than on the line. ICSA-26-246-02 covers the IXON VPN Client, where CVE-2026-75925 allows remote code execution with elevated privileges on the machine running the client in versions before 1.4.7 — the usual way a filler, packer or refrigeration OEM reaches the plant. ICSA-26-246-03 covers Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH at V15.07 and earlier, where CVE-2026-12663 lets commands or code run at the logged-in user’s permission level; ControlFLASH is how firmware reaches the controllers behind processing, packaging and cold-chain equipment. ICSA-26-246-06 covers Inductive Automation Ignition, where any authenticated user can create projects. None is reported as exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-246-02 (IXON VPN Client), ICSA-26-246-03 (Rockwell Automation ControlFLASH) and ICSA-26-246-06 (Inductive Automation Ignition) - Published 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10 pre-auth flaw in SonicWall’s SMA1000 remote-access gateway is being exploited, and CISA gave agencies three days
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall disclosed on 1 September that two previously unknown vulnerabilities in its SMA1000 secure remote access gateway and SSL-VPN appliance are being exploited in the wild; the company says it found both the flaws and the exploitation internally. CVE-2026-83548, scored CVSS 10, is a pre-authentication server-side request forgery in the Appliance Work Place interface. CVE-2026-83549, at 7.8, is an operating-system command injection flaw in the Appliance Management Console. Chained, the pair gives an unauthenticated attacker remote code execution on the appliance itself. CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2 September with a 5 September deadline for federal civilian agencies, and marked both entries as requiring forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 — a signal that patching alone does not close the incident. Affected models are the SMA1000 6210, 7210 and 8200v; SSL-VPN running on SonicWall firewalls and the SMA 100 series are not affected. - SonicWall PSIRT advisory and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition of 2 Sep 2026 — corroborated by SecurityWeek, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security and Sophos - Vendor advisory published 1 Sep 2026; added to CISA KEV 2 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 1 September ICS batch is mostly Rockwell — and it reaches the Logix controllers themselves
item.category: Critical Advisory — Vendor patch available
item.description: CISA published eight industrial control system advisories on 1 September, and five of them are Rockwell Automation. The one most sites will notice first is ICSA-26-244-01, covering four denial-of-service flaws in RSLinx Classic 4.50 and earlier — CVE-2026-9621, CVE-2026-9622, CVE-2026-9624 and CVE-2026-9625. All four are remotely triggerable with no authentication and no user interaction: a single crafted Common Industrial Protocol packet crashes the RSLinx Classic service. Rockwell has fixed all four in version 4.60. The rest of the batch covers the Redundancy Module Configuration Tool (ICSA-26-244-02), the Logix platform (-03, reaching ControlLogix 5580, CompactLogix 5380, GuardLogix 5580 and Compact GuardLogix 5380), FactoryTalk Activation Manager (-04) and the ControlLogix, CompactLogix, CompactLogix 5480, GuardLogix and Compact GuardLogix controller families (-05). No exploitation has been reported for any of them. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-244-01 through ICSA-26-244-05, published 1 Sep 2026, cross-checked against the Rockwell Automation security advisory index - Advisories published 1 Sep 2026 — verified 3 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A print server chained to unauthenticated code execution — PaperCut’s zero-day pair lands in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: PaperCut confirmed on 27 August that it was investigating active exploitation of its NG and MF print-management products, and assigned CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 the following day. The first lets an unauthenticated attacker reach the Application Server and change its configuration; the second turns that change into arbitrary code execution through unsafe reflection. Chained, they give a network-adjacent attacker code execution with no credentials at all, and CISA added both to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 31 August. Print management almost never appears on an OT asset register. The server usually does hold a domain service account, does sit on the same segment as engineering workstations, and is reachable from nearly every host in the estate — which makes it a convenient staging point rather than a target in its own right. Arctic Wolf reported on 6 September that it is seeing the chain used in practice: after gaining execution, operators run reconnaissance, create privileged accounts and harvest credentials and PaperCut configuration secrets — behaviour consistent with establishing a durable foothold rather than a smash-and-grab. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog addition and the PaperCut security bulletin — corroborated by SecurityWeek, Help Net Security, Rapid7 and The Hacker News - Vendor disclosed active exploitation 27 Aug 2026; CVEs assigned 28 Aug 2026; added to KEV 31 Aug 2026; post-exploitation activity reported by Arctic Wolf 6 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Fuel-Boss ships with end-of-life web components — a reminder of what sits behind the farm and depot fuel island
item.category: Advisory — Fuel management at farms, depots and processing sites
item.description: CISA’s 27 August batch includes All-Line Equipment Company’s Fuel-Boss, the fuel management and dispensing control system used at agricultural co-operatives, grain and feed operations, trucking depots and processing sites to authorise and log fuel draws. The advisory documents two flaws inherited from bundled end-of-life components: an argument-injection issue in the University of Washington IMAP toolkit as reached through PHP’s imap_open(), which allows remote command execution, and a buffer-handling flaw in PHP-FPM configurations up to and including PHP 7.1.5 that can produce a remote code execution condition. Neither is exotic; both are the predictable result of an embedded web stack that stopped receiving updates years ago. For a food and agriculture operator the exposure is practical rather than dramatic — fuel dispatch controls harvest logistics and cold-chain haulage, and an unavailable fuel island stops trucks. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-239-02, published in the 27 Aug 2026 batch of seven advisories — corroborated by the WaterISAC weekly roundup - Published 27 Aug 2026; verified 30 Aug 2026

item.title: [High] Three more exploited flaws land in KEV — a Linux kernel bug, a JFrog Artifactory path traversal and a two-year-old ownCloud authentication bypass
item.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue
item.description: CISA added three more actively exploited flaws to the KEV catalogue on 27 August, a day after the six-flaw batch containing NetScaler. None is an ICS product, and in food and beverage that is exactly how production stops: Fairlife’s July shutdown and the wider ransomware pattern the Food and Ag-ISAC tracks both start in enterprise IT. CVE-2026-53362 is a Linux kernel flaw, and the MES and warehouse-management server, historian, vision system, label printer controller and OT network sensor in most plants are Linux underneath — usually vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s timetable. CVE-2026-66384 is a path traversal in JFrog Artifactory, relevant where firmware or automation packages destined for line equipment are staged. CVE-2023-49105 is an ownCloud authentication bypass patched since late 2023; instances still exposed are typically unowned. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition, corroborated by Security Affairs and SecurityWeek - Added to KEV 27 Aug 2026; ownCloud flaw originally disclosed Nov 2023

item.title: [Critical] The NetScaler flaw is now confirmed exploited and in KEV — federal deadline 29 August
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, CISA KEV, remote access
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-8452 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 26 August, moving the Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway issue from a patching recommendation to confirmed exploitation in the wild. It is a heap overflow in SAML single sign-on parsing, rated CVSS 8.8, requiring no authentication, and reachable when the appliance is configured as a Gateway or AAA virtual server. Canada’s Cyber Centre reported indications of exploitation from around 17 August after a public proof of concept. In food manufacturing NetScaler commonly fronts the remote access used by plant engineers, out-of-hours support and the OEMs who dial in to fillers, packaging lines and refrigeration. Exploitation has not tailed off: reporting on 5 September describes continued attempts against the authentication bypass from multiple geolocations, so an appliance patched late should be treated as possibly already touched rather than simply late. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue addition of 26 Aug 2026 and Citrix security bulletin CTX696939 — corroborated by the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and watchTowr Labs analysis - Vendor bulletin published 20 Aug 2026; exploitation indications from 17 Aug; added to KEV 26 Aug 2026; federal deadline 29 Aug 2026; continued exploitation reported 5 Sep 2026; verified 7 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA makes the case for decoys — a detection method you can add without touching the process
item.category: Guidance — Detection method for critical infrastructure networks
item.description: CISA published “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. The premise is unsentimental: assume an attacker will eventually obtain some access, and plant assets whose only purpose is to be touched by someone who should not be there. The guide covers tripwires, breadcrumbs and honeytokens, positions them alongside Zero Trust rather than instead of it, and structures the work in three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — to be iterated with red-team exercises. Planning is framed around the three MITRE Engage goals of expose, affect and elicit, with detections mapped to ATT&CK and deliberate attention to the living-off-the-land activity that signature-based tooling misses. Industrial Cyber’s coverage reports a detailed water and wastewater case study in the document, including decoys placed to look like OT HMIs; SecurityWeek’s write-up does not mention water or OT, so treat the OT case study as that outlet’s reporting until you have read the PDF. The reason this suits food and beverage plants is the one thing decoys do not require: a change to a live control system. A fake historian share, a false engineering-workstation credential or an HMI-looking host on the plant VLAN costs no production risk and no vendor sign-off. - CISA, “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — reported by Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek; the water and wastewater case study is Industrial Cyber’s reporting - Guidance published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA retires its weekly vulnerability bulletin on 28 September — check whether your process reads it
item.category: Policy — Source change for vulnerability management teams
item.description: CISA is discontinuing its weekly Vulnerability Summary bulletin with effect from 28 September 2026, reported on 17 September. The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, alerts and advisories all continue; the change is framed as consistent with the risk-based prioritisation set out in Binding Operational Directive 26-04 in June 2026. Nothing in the reporting indicates that ICS advisories are affected. For food and beverage operators the practical question is narrow and easy to check: does anything in your vulnerability-management routine, or in a managed service provider’s, consume that weekly bulletin as a feed or as the trigger for a review meeting? Small and mid-sized processors in particular tend to have one person who reads a weekly digest rather than a subscription to per-advisory feeds, and a source that stops arriving quietly is worse than one that stops loudly. - CISA announcement as reported by SecurityWeek; KEV, alerts and advisories are unaffected - Reported 17 Sep 2026; bulletin retired 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] ENISA switches on the Single Reporting Platform as the Cyber Resilience Act’s vulnerability reporting duties take effect
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity deployed the initial operating capability of its Single Reporting Platform, announced 14 September, giving manufacturers and open-source software stewards the channel they need to meet Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations that took effect this month. Under the CRA, makers of products with digital elements must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents on a defined clock, with an early warning followed by a fuller notification. Food and beverage processors are beneficiaries rather than regulated parties, unless they place connected products on the EU market themselves. The practical gain is faster, more consistent vulnerability disclosure from the vendors of line control, packaging and cold-chain equipment. Reported here factually as a regulatory milestone, without comment on the underlying policy debate. - ENISA announcement of the Single Reporting Platform initial operating capability — reporting via Industrial Cyber - Announced and reported 14 Sep 2026; CRA reporting obligations effective September 2026

item.title: [Info] EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting went live on 11 September — your line and refrigeration vendors now have 24 hours
item.category: Regulation & Policy — EU, now in force
item.description: The vulnerability and incident reporting obligations of the EU Cyber Resilience Act took effect on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements must now notify an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe security incident through ENISA’s Single Reporting Platform within 24 hours of becoming aware, follow up within 72 hours with exploit and mitigation detail, and file a final report within 14 days of a fix becoming available, as well as informing affected users. It applies to manufacturers placing products on the EU market wherever they are based, with penalties up to €15 million. For a food or beverage processor this cuts two ways. Your filling, packaging, palletising, refrigeration and ag-IoT suppliers — many of them European — are now on a 24-hour clock, so you should hear about exploited flaws sooner. And if your group builds or badges any connected product sold into Europe, the obligation may apply to you directly. - European Commission CRA reporting guidance and ENISA Single Reporting Platform — reported by Dark Reading - Obligations in force from 11 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] 117 federal cyber incident reporting rules, and the argument that they pull staff off the response
item.category: Policy — Incident reporting burden, CIRCIA rules pending
item.description: The McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce published analysis on 8 September counting, from GAO figures, 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations spread across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. Their argument is operational rather than political: in the first hours of an incident, the people who understand the affected systems are the same people drafting duplicate notifications in different formats to different regulators on different clocks. The timing matters because CIRCIA’s implementing rules are expected to be finalised this autumn. A food or agriculture business feels this acutely if it also handles payment card data, holds regulated financial or health information, ships product to state agencies, or operates in the EU alongside NIS2 and Cyber Resilience Act duties — a single ransomware event at a processing site can trigger several clocks at once. - McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis citing GAO figures — reported by Industrial Cyber - Published 8 Sep 2026; CIRCIA implementing rules expected to be finalised autumn 2026

item.title: [Medium] The free assessment small operators actually used is being withdrawn — and nothing at that price replaces it
item.category: Policy — CISA reported to be ending six free critical-infrastructure assessment services
item.description: Cybersecurity Dive reported on 3 September that CISA has told staff to stop delivering six of the free assessment services it has offered critical-infrastructure owners, including its on-site architecture design review and several facilitated risk and resilience assessments, following an internal direction reportedly given on 25 August. The agency had not published a formal notice as of this edition, so the exact scope and end dates should be read as reported rather than confirmed. For food and agriculture the loss falls on mid-market processors, co-operatives and grain handlers that sit inside a designated critical-infrastructure sector but carry no dedicated security staff, and who used these engagements as the external review their customers and insurers keep asking about. - Cybersecurity Dive reporting, carried by Utility Dive — based on an internal CISA meeting described by people familiar with it; no formal agency notice had been published as of this edition - Direction reportedly given 25 Aug 2026; reported 3 Sep 2026 — verified 6 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] OpenAI pledges $1bn of subsidised AI defence for critical-infrastructure operators — terms not yet published
item.category: Regulation & Policy — Industry initiative
item.description: OpenAI said on 4 September that it will commit $1 billion to an initiative it calls Daybreak, offering subsidised AI cyber capabilities, training and technical assistance to defenders of critical infrastructure. Cost, eligibility and what “subsidised” means in practice have not been published, and no delivery timeline has been given. Food and agriculture is exactly the kind of sector such a programme is aimed at — the Food and Ag-ISAC’s own 3 September report argues that AI-assisted monitoring is one of the few realistic ways to surface a shadow-OT estate nobody has the staff to inventory by hand. Note it and wait for terms. When they appear, read them as you would any third party asking for telemetry from a processing line or a cold store, because that is the data involved. - SecurityWeek reporting on OpenAI’s Daybreak announcement - Announced and reported 4 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Six agencies publish outage-communication guidance for IT and OT service providers — and a processor is one to its retailers
item.category: Policy — Joint international guidance, incident communications
item.description: On 2 September the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security joined CISA, Australia’s ASD ACSC, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK and the FBI to publish joint guidance on communicating during IT and OT service outages, titled “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers.” It asks for a written incident communications plan with defined trigger thresholds and named audiences, plain-language updates, root-cause and technical detail end users can act on, and messaging aligned with legal and regulatory duties. Food and agriculture has a harder version of this problem than most sectors, because the audience is not only customers. A production stoppage raises supply questions for retailers, allocation questions for distributors and, where the affected product is perishable or refrigerated, food-safety questions that regulators expect to be answered quickly and precisely. - Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and CISA — joint guidance “Communicating Under Pressure: Best Practices for Service Providers” - Published 2 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] From 11 September 2026 exploited vulnerabilities in digital products must be reported within 24 hours
item.category: Policy — EU Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligation
item.description: The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations begin on 11 September 2026. Manufacturers of products with digital elements placed on the EU market must notify an actively exploited vulnerability in their product, or a severe incident affecting its security, within 24 hours of becoming aware, with fuller reporting to follow. Food and agriculture businesses are mostly buyers here, and that is the useful angle: the suppliers of fillers, packaging lines, refrigeration controllers, weighing systems and ag-IoT platforms sold into Europe acquire a defined notification duty that can be written into support contracts. - European Commission guidance on Cyber Resilience Act reporting obligations (Regulation 2024/2847) - Obligations apply from 11 Sep 2026; phase-start reporting reviewed 1 Sep 2026; re-verified 4 Sep 2026
